Adult South Pacific hake (Merluccius gayi) are known to attain a maximum total length of 87 centimeters [Li = 87 centimeters], a size that distinguishes this species as a moderately large member of the Merlucciidae family. Field surveys conducted along the continental shelf of Chile and Peru have documented individuals approaching this upper limit, though the majority of the spawning stock consists of fish ranging considerably smaller. The wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae has been estimated at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a value derived from the measured egg diameter of approximately 900 micrometers, which yields a minute spherical volume prior to chorion hydration. This extremely low initial mass places the hatchlings among the more diminutive gadiform larvae and imposes a tight energetic constraint during the transition to first exogenous feeding. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva must begin absorbing its endogenous reserves rapidly, as the window for successful prey capture is brief in the cold upwelling waters that typify its nursery grounds.

Female South Pacific hake reach sexual maturity at a total length of 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 570 grams [Wwp = approximately 570 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from local fisheries data. This size threshold is typically attained between the second and third year of life, after which vitellogenesis commences and the HPG axis becomes fully activated. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is tightly linked to seasonal oceanographic conditions, with spawning aggregations forming during the austral winter when upwelling intensity is at its peak. The ultimate wet weight recorded for this species reaches 12164 grams [Wwi = 12164 grams], an asymptotic mass that is achieved only by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. Such large fish are disproportionately represented in deeper, offshore habitats where fishing pressure is somewhat reduced compared to the coastal spawning zones.

Under thermal conditions characteristic of the species' primary distribution range, specifically at a stable water temperature of 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C], the maximum reproductive output of South Pacific hake has been quantified through examination of batch fecundity and spawning interval data. Each mature female produces approximately 1,918 eggs per spawning batch [N_R_i = approximately 1,918 eggs per spawning batch] and spawns at a rate of up to one batch per day, resulting in a daily reproductive output of 1,918 eggs per day [Ri = 1,918 eggs per day]. This high fecundity is typical of demersal-spawning gadoids. The reproductive strategy involves multiple batch spawnings throughout the extended spawning season, allowing females to spread the risk of egg mortality across different hydrographic conditions and thereby enhancing overall reproductive success in a variable environment.

The maximum recorded lifespan for South Pacific hake is 20 years [am = 20 years], a longevity that places it among the longer-lived members of the genus Merluccius when environmental temperatures remain near the population mean of 10.9 °C [T = 10.9 °C]. This extended life span allows individuals to accumulate substantial somatic mass over many reproductive seasons, with the largest females contributing disproportionately to the annual egg production of the stock. The senescent adult stage is rarely observed in commercial catches, as fishing mortality typically removes most individuals well before they reach the upper age limit. Growth increments slow considerably after the first decade, with annual length increases becoming negligible as fish approach their asymptotic size. This pattern is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes reproductive output over continued rapid somatic expansion once a critical body size has been attained.

A notable feature of the genus Merluccius is the range of size at first maturation: M. gayi, at 32 centimeters [Lp = 32 centimeters] total length for females, occupies an intermediate position, falling below values for Merluccius productus but above those for Merluccius bilinearis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, predicted at 570 grams [Wwp = 570 grams], reflects the energetic investment required before vitellogenesis begins. The larval wet weight at birth of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] is consistent with the low maternal investment per offspring typical of broadcast-spawning gadoids, where fecundity is maximized at the expense of per-egg provisioning. Collectively, these life-history parameters describe a species that balances relatively rapid early growth and early maturation with a prolonged reproductive window, a combination that has proven successful in the dynamic oceanographic environment it occupies.
